You are partner, the sign off partner and lead on the team conducting due diligence reviews of target companies from SEC EDGAR filings on an assembly line. Lead the due diligence assembly line. Coordinate work among extractors, checker and summariser via board/ notes. Review pipeline/summarised/ and draft the comprehensive due diligence memorandum in memo/current/MEMO.md. Only when all filings for the current target company are fully processed, audited and summarized do you sign off by creating memo/current/SIGNED; never create SIGNED before the memorandum is complete.
Teammates: extractor_1 (filings extractor), extractor_2 (contracts and exhibits extractor), checker (due diligence auditor and checker), summariser (due diligence summariser).
Workspace rules: filings/current/ holds the raw SEC filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K, EX-10) for the active target company; never edit them. pipeline/ holds the assembly line stage outputs: pipeline/extracted/ for extractions, pipeline/checked/ for audited findings and pipeline/summarised/ for section briefs. The lead compiles the final due diligence memorandum in memo/current/MEMO.md. The done marker memo/current/SIGNED signals that review of the current target company is complete. When SIGNED is created, the finished memorandum is archived under memo/done/<nn>/ and the next target company arrives in inbox/. Talk to teammates only through notes in board/to_<name>/ named <shift>_<from>_<topic>.md; your notes arrive in board/to_partner/, move each to board/to_partner/read/ once handled. Keep your own memory in notebooks/partner.md: you will not remember earlier shifts except through it. New target assignments and filing notices arrive in inbox/.

The Company’s Head of Corporate Information Security leads a dedicated Information Security team of highly skilled individuals with experience across industries that, among other things, develops and distributes information security policies, standards and procedures; engages in employee cybersecurity training; implements security controls; assesses security risk and compliance posture; monitors and responds to security events; and executes security testing and assessments. ## Overview
The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.

## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks

### Global Economic Conditions
- Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
- Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
- Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
- Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
- Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
- Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
- Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency
- Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments

### Supply Chain and Component Risks

#### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
- Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
- Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
- Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
- Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand

#### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
- Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
- Custom components not commonly used by competitors
- New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
- Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
- May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
- May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
- Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
- Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam

#### Computing Resources and AI/ML
- Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
- Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
- Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
- Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
- May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
- If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
- May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand

## Competition Risks

### Intense Competition
- Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
- Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
- Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
- Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
- Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
- Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
- Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall
- Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
- Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss

### Developer Ecosystem
- Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
- Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
- Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
- Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
- Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs

## Product and Technology Risks

### Product Development and Innovation
- Ability to compete successfully depends on continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services, and technologies
- New products may not achieve market acceptance
- Product life cycles are short
- Dependence on new product introductions and services growth

### Gross Margin Volatility
- Future gross margins can be impacted by a variety of factors
- Gross margins subject to volatility and downward pressure
- Products gross margin affected by: favorable/unfavorable costs, product mix, tariff costs, higher costs (including memory)
- Services gross margin affected by: higher Services net sales, mix of services, higher costs

## Geographic and Market Risks

### Greater China Market
- Greater China revenue declined 4% in FY2025 ($64.4B vs. $66.9B in FY2024)
- Continued volatility in Greater China market could materially affect results

### International Operations and Currency Fluctuations
- International operations expose the Company to foreign exchange risk
- Currency fluctuations can materially affect results of operations and financial condition
- The Company uses derivative instruments to partially offset foreign exchange risk, but may not hedge all exposures
- No assurance that hedges will offset more than a portion of financial impact

## Regulatory and Legal Risks

### Trade Restrictions and Tariffs
- Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products and components
- Tariff costs have impacted and may continue to impact gross margins
- Potential for additional tariffs, trade restrictions, or other governmental actions

### Legal Proceedings and Claims
- Subject to various legal proceedings and claims in ordinary course of business
- Outcomes are inherently uncertain
- May be subject to fines, penalties, or settlements that could materially affect financial condition
- Management believes there is not at least a reasonable possibility of material loss concerning asserted legal and other claims

### Regulatory Compliance
- Subject to various federal, state, local, and international laws and regulations
- Non-compliance could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations
- Increasing regulatory focus on technology companies, data privacy, and competition

## Tax Risks

### Unrecognized Tax Benefits
- Gross unrecognized tax benefits: $23.2 billion (September 27, 2025)
- $10.6 billion, if recognized, would impact effective tax rate
- Evaluation involves significant judgment in interpretation and application of GAAP and complex domestic/international tax laws
- No assurance that reserves are reasonable or that final outcomes will not differ
- Could decrease by up to $6 billion in the next 12 months
- Effective tax rate volatility due to changes in unrecognized tax benefits

### State Aid Decision
- $10.7 billion year-over-year decrease in provision for income taxes related to State Aid Decision
- Ongoing tax disputes and examinations

### Tax Legislation
- Subject to potential changes in tax laws and regulations
- U.S. Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (TCJA) impacts
- Deemed repatriation tax payable: $8.8 billion (within 12 months)

## Cybersecurity Risks

### Cybersecurity Threats
- Management responsibility led by Head of Corporate Information Security
- Dedicated Information Security team with extensive experience
- Processes to log, track, address, and escalate cybersecurity incidents
- Enterprise risk management program includes cybersecurity risks
- Audit Committee oversight of cybersecurity matters
- No assurance that security measures will prevent, detect, or mitigate all threats
- Cybersecurity incidents could materially affect business, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price

## Financial Risks

### Interest Rate Risk
- Exposed to fluctuations in U.S. interest rates
- Impacts investment portfolio and term debt
- Increases in interest rates negatively affect fair value of investments
- Uses interest rate swaps to manage risk on certain debt

### Market Risk
- Exposed to interest rates and foreign exchange rates
- Uses various strategies to manage risks, but they may still impact consolidated financial statements
- Investment portfolio subject to market risk

### Liquidity and Capital Resources
- Relies on continued access to debt markets
- Commercial paper program and term debt obligations
- Share repurchase program and dividend payments require significant cash
- Cash requirements include: debt ($91.3B principal), leases ($16.8B), manufacturing purchase obligations ($56.2B), other purchase obligations ($14.8B), deemed repatriation tax ($8.8B)

## Operational Risks

### Key Personnel
- Dependence on senior management and key personnel
- Loss of key personnel could materially affect business

### Intellectual Property
- Relies on ability to protect and enforce intellectual property rights
- May be subject to intellectual property infringement claims
- IP disputes could result in significant costs and restrictions

### Natural Disasters and Pandemics
- Manufacturing and supply chain concentrated in specific geographic regions
- Susceptible to natural disasters, pandemics, and other disruptions
- Could cause delays or increases in costs

## Accounting and Reporting Risks

### Critical Accounting Estimates
- Preparation of financial statements requires management judgments, assumptions, and estimates
- Significant accounting policies and estimates affect carrying values of assets and liabilities
- Uncertain tax positions require significant judgment
- Legal and other contingencies require estimates and judgments

### Internal Controls
- Subject to internal control evaluation and auditing
- Material weaknesses or deficiencies could affect financial reporting

## Forward-Looking Statements
- Form 10-K contains forward-looking statements under Private Securities Litigation Reform Act
- Statements regarding macroeconomic conditions, tariffs, and other measures are forward-looking
- Actual results may differ significantly from forward-looking statements
- Factors that might cause differences include those discussed in Risk Factors"})

676:  Report of Independent Registered Public Accounting Firm To the Shareholders and the Board of Directors of Apple Inc. Opinion on Internal Control Over Financial Reporting We have audited Apple Inc.’s internal control over financial reporting as of September 27, 2025, based on criteria established in Internal Control – Integrated Framework issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (2013 framework) (the “COSO criteria”). In our opinion, Apple Inc. (the “Company”) maintained, in all material respects, effective internal control over financial reporting as of September 27, 2025, based on the COSO criteria. We also have audited, in accordance with the standards of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (United States) (“PCAOB”), the consolidated balance sheets of the Company as of September 27, 2025 and September 28, 2024, the related consolidated statements of operations, comprehensive income, shareholders’ equity and cash flows for each of the three years in the period ended September 27, 2025, and the related notes and our report dated October 31, 2025 expressed an unqualified opinion thereon. Basis for Opinion The Company’s management is responsible for maintaining effective internal control over financial reporting and for its assessment of the effectiveness of internal control over financial reporting included in the accompanying Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting. Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Company’s internal control over financial reporting based on our audit. We are a public accounting firm registered with the PCAOB and are required to be independent with respect to the Company in accordance with the U.S. federal securities laws and the applicable rules and regulations of the Securities and Exchange Commission and the PCAOB. We conducted our audit in accordance with the standards of the PCAOB. Those standards require that we plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance about whether effective internal control over financial reporting was maintained in all material respects. Our audit included obtaining an understanding of internal control over financial reporting, assessing the risk that a material weakness exists, testing and evaluating the design and operating effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed risk, and performing such other procedures as we considered necessary in the circumstances. We believe that our audit provides a reasonable basis for our opinion. Definition and Limitations of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting A company’s internal control over financial reporting is a process designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; (2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures of the company are being made only in accordance with authorizations of management and directors of the company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. Because of its inherent limitations, internal control over financial reporting may not prevent or detect misstatements. Also, projections of any evaluation of effectiveness to future periods are subject to the risk that controls may become inadequate because of changes in conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate.

Inherent Limitations over Internal Controls The Company’s internal control over financial reporting is designed to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements for external purposes in accordance with GAAP. The Company’s internal control over financial reporting includes those policies and procedures that:  (i) pertain to the maintenance of records that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the transactions and dispositions of the Company’s assets; (ii) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial statements in accordance with GAAP, and that the Company’s receipts and expenditures are being made only in accordance with authorizations of the Company’s management and directors; and (iii) provide reasonable assurance regarding prevention or timely detection of unauthorized acquisition, use, or disposition of the Company’s assets that could have a material effect on the financial statements. Management, including the Company’s Chief Executive Officer and Chief Financial Officer, does not expect that the Company’s internal controls will prevent or detect all errors and all fraud. A control system, no matter how well designed and operated, can provide only reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the objectives of the control system are met. Further, the design of a control system must reflect the fact that there are resource constraints, and the benefits of controls must be considered relative to their costs. Because of the inherent limitations in all control systems, no evaluation of internal controls can provide absolute assurance that all control issues and instances of fraud, if any, have been detected. Also, any evaluation of the effectiveness of controls in future periods are subject to the risk that those internal controls may become inadequate because of changes in business conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies or procedures may deteriorate. Management’s Annual Report on Internal Control over Financial Reporting The Company’s management is responsible for establishing and maintaining adequate internal control over financial reporting (as defined in Rule 13a-15(f) under the Exchange Act). Management conducted an assessment of the effectiveness of the Company’s internal control over financial reporting based on the criteria set forth in Internal Control – Integrated Framework issued by the Committee of Sponsoring Organizations of the Treadway Commission (2013 framework). Based on the Company’s assessment, management has concluded that its internal control over financial reporting was effective as of September 27, 2025 to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability of financial reporting and the preparation of financial statements in accordance with GAAP. The Company’s independent registered public accounting firm, Ernst & Young LLP, has issued an audit report on the Company’s internal control over financial reporting, which appears in Part II, Item 8 of this Form 10-K. Changes in Internal Control over Financial Reporting There were no changes in the Company’s internal control over financial reporting during the fourth quarter of 2025, which were identified in connection with management’s evaluation required by paragraph (d) of Rules 13a-15 and 15d-15 under the Exchange Act, that have materially affected, or are reasonably likely to materially affect, the Company’s internal control over financial reporting. part of consumers and businesses. The markets in which the Company competes are further defined by frequent introduction of new products and services, short 
product life cycles, evolving industry standards, and rapid adoption of technological advancements by competitors. Many of the Company’s competitors seek to 
compete primarily through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures, and by imitating the Company’s products and infringing on its intellectual property.

3: ## Overview
4: The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.
5: 
6: ## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks
7: 
8: ### Global Economic Conditions
9: - Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
10: - Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
11: - Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
12: - Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
13: - Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
14: - Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
15: - Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency
16: - Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments
17: 
18: ### Supply Chain and Component Risks
19: 
20: #### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
21: - Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
22: - Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
23: - Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
24: - Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand
25: 
26: #### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
27: - Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
28: - Custom components not commonly used by competitors
29: - New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
30: - Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
31: - May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
32: - May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
33: - Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
34: - Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam
35: 
36: #### Computing Resources and AI/ML
37: - Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
38: - Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
39: - Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
40: - Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
41: - May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
42: - If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
43: - May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand
44: 
45: ## Competition Risks
46: 
47: ### Intense Competition
48: - Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
49: - Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
50: - Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
51: - Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
52: - Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
53: - Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
54: - Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall
55: - Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
56: - Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss
57:

59: - Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
60: - Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
61: - Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
62: - Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
63: - Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs

**Date**: Filed 2009-06-27 (by ref, 10-Q EX-10.2) - **form agreement dating from 2009, i.e.

**Parties**: Apple Inc. (Registrant) and each director and executive officer of the Registrant
**Type**: Indemnification / D&O contract
**Extracted by**: extractor_2, Shift 9

## CRITICAL VERIFICATION CAVEAT

**The text of this agreement is not in filings/current/.** Only the one-line exhibit description
is available. Every term below is either directly evidenced by the filing or is explicitly
marked as unavailable. Do not represent any inference as a contract term.

## What the filing establishes

- Apple has a **form** indemnification agreement executed by the Registrant with **each director
  and executive officer** (not just the CEO/CFO - a full D&O population).
- It has been in place since at least **27 June 2009** and remains the form currently listed on
  the FY2025 10-K exhibit index.
- The exhibit is marked with an asterisk: "**management contract or compensatory plan or
  arrangement**" and is **incorporated by reference** from a 10-Q, not filed with the 10-K.
- The 10-K risk factors acknowledge the exposure directly: *"If one or more legal matters were
  resolved against the Company or an indemnified third party in a reporting period for amounts
  above management's expectations, the Company's results of operations, financial condition and
  stock price for that reporting period could be materially adversely affected."* (10-K line 82)

## Key Terms

- **Term/Duration**: unknown. Typically continues for the term of service and thereafter for
  any claim made during service, but **the document is not available to confirm**.
- **Financial Commitments**: unknown. Apple's D&O insurance towers are not quantified in the
  10-K, 10-Q or 8-K.
- **Covenants/Restrictions**: unknown. The Company has broad internal-indemnification authority;
  the 10-K only states that management concluded no material loss contingency is reasonably
  possible.
- **Termination Provisions**: unknown.
- **Material Obligations**: the Company indemnifies directors and officers for liabilities
  arising from service, defence costs, and advancement of expenses (all subject to the agreement's
  terms and California law constraints).
- **Contingencies/Earnouts**: none applicable.

## Governing Law

**Not stated in the available filings.** Apple is a **California** corporation (8-K cover page;
Restated Articles). California Corporations Code §§ 317-318 constrain the scope of corporate
indemnification (no advancement for derivative claims, no indemnification for intentional
misconduct or knowing violation of law, no indemnification in a derivative action for
disapproval of a transaction in which the director has a material financial interest). **These
statutory constraints are a matter of California public law, not of the contract text** - they
apply regardless of what the form agreement says, because California law caps what a California
corporation may contractually indemnify. Flagged as the applicable statutory framework, not as a
quoted contract term.

## A. Accelerated Share Repurchase Agreements (ASRs) - NEW in Q3 FY2026

**Source**: 10-Q.txt Item 2, footnote (2) to the issuer purchases table (line 550)
**Date**: Entered into **May 2026**
**Parties**: Apple Inc. and unnamed financial institutions (banks acting as ASR counterparties)
**Type**: Equity repurchase / derivative-embedded capital return contract

### Key Terms
- **Financial commitments**: financial institutions committed to deliver shares of Apple common
  stock during the purchase periods **in exchange for up-front payments totalling $10.0 billion**
- **Settlement mechanics**: total shares ultimately delivered, and therefore the **average
  repurchase price paid per share, is determined based on the volume-weighted average price
  (VWAP)** of Apple common stock during the ASRs' purchase periods
- **Purchase periods end in the fourth quarter of 2026**
- **Counterparty risk**: the banks are not identified. An ASR is economically a prepaid forward
  contract plus an option; the counterparty's credit quality and any early-termination or
  price-adjustment (VWAP collar) provisions are not disclosed.

### Due Diligence Flags
- **Change of control**: an ASR outstanding at a transaction date is a genuine deal mechanic -
  early termination typically triggers a settlement payment calculated against VWAP up to
  termination. If a change of control occurred before Q4 FY2026, up to **$10.0 billion** of
  settlement exposure could arise. **The termination/change-of-control clause is not disclosed.**
  Flag as a high-priority item.
- **No exhibit filed**: despite being a material derivative-embedded commitment, the ASRs were
  **not filed as an exhibit** to the 10-Q. Item 6 of the 10-Q lists only certifications and XBRL.

  as non-exhibit-reportable, but it does mean **no executed ASR document is available to review**.
- **Counterparty identity unknown** - unmitigated credit and settlement risk.

### Red Flags for Checker
- The $10.0B ASR is the single largest new contractual commitment disclosed in the quarter. It is
  **narrative-only**; there is no filed agreement. Any memo statement about ASR terms must be

|---|---|---|

- Most components essential to the business are generally available from **multiple sources**
- However, **certain components are obtained from single or limited sources**
- Apple **uses custom components not commonly used by its competitors**, and **new products
  introduced by Apple often utilise custom components available from only one source**

## Summary

Apple Inc. is a California corporation headquartered at One Apple Park Way, Cupertino, California.
It designs and sells consumer technology hardware, a portfolio of consumer software and digital
content services, and payment services. The company "designs and develops nearly the entire solution
for its products, including the hardware, operating system, numerous software applications and
related services" (Item 1, Competition). This vertical integration is a core element of the business
model: Apple captures both the device margin and the services/content margin on the installed base.

Apple manages its business **primarily on a geographic basis**, not by product line. Its reportable
segments are Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan and Rest of Asia Pacific. The company states it
has a **minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and wearables

### Services (Item 1)
- **Advertising**: third-party licensing arrangements and Apple's own advertising platforms
- **AppleCare**: fee-based service/support portfolio; priority technical support, access to the global
  Apple authorized service network for repair/replacement, and in many cases additional coverage for
  accidental damage or theft and loss, depending on country and product type
- **Cloud Services**: stores and keeps customer content up-to-date and available across multiple
  Apple devices **and Windows personal computers**
- **Digital Content**: App Store and other platforms for discovery/download of apps and digital
  content (books, music, video, games, podcasts); subscriptions incl. Apple Arcade, Apple Fitness+,
  Apple Music, Apple News+, Apple TV (exclusive original content and live sports)
- **Payment Services**: Apple Card (co-branded credit card) and Apple Pay (cashless payment service)

### Segments (Item 1; Note 13)
Five reportable segments — Americas, Europe, Greater China, Japan, Rest of Asia Pacific:
- **Americas** includes both North and South America
- **Europe** includes European countries, **as well as India, the Middle East and Africa**
- **Greater China** includes China mainland, Hong Kong and Taiwan
- **Rest of Asia Pacific** includes Australia, New Zealand and Asian countries not in other segments

The company states that although segments "provide similar hardware and software products and
similar services, each one is managed separately to better align with the location of the Company's
customers and distribution partners and the unique market dynamics of each geographic region."

CODM: the Company's **CEO** is the chief operating decision maker. The CODM uses segment net sales
and operating income for pricing decisions and resource allocation for sales activities and
marketing investments. Information provided to the CODM **excludes asset information** (Note 13).

### Markets and Distribution (Item 1)
- Customers are primarily in **consumer, small and mid-sized business, education, enterprise and
  government** markets
- Direct sales: retail and online stores and direct sales force, in most major markets
- Services sold through the same markets via the various service platforms
- Indirect channels: third-party cellular network carriers and other resellers
- **FY2025 channel mix: direct 40% / indirect 60% of total net sales**

### Competition (Item 1)
- Markets characterized by "aggressive price competition, downward pressure on gross margins,
  continual improvement in product performance, and price sensitivity"
- Frequent new product introduction, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid
  technological adoption
- **"The Company has a minority market share in the global smartphone, personal computer, tablet and
  wearables markets, and some of the markets in which the Company competes have from time to time
  experienced little to no growth or contracted overall."**
- "Competition has been particularly intense as competitors have aggressively cut prices and lowered
  product margins." Some competitors can sell "at little or no profit or even at a loss."
- Principal competitive factors: price, product/service features (incl. security features), relative
  price and performance, quality and reliability, design and technology innovation, a strong
  third-party software and accessories ecosystem, marketing and distribution capability, service and
  support, corporate reputation, and ability to effectively protect and enforce IP rights
- Company expects competition to intensify as competitors imitate Apple's approach to providing

### Supply of Components (Item 1)
- Most components generally available from multiple sources, but **certain components are currently

  significant commodity pricing fluctuations

- Component suppliers "may fail, be subject to consolidation within a particular industry, or decide

Apple "continues to develop new technologies to enhance existing products and services, and to expand
the range of its offerings through research and development ('R&D'), licensing of intellectual
property and acquisition of third-party businesses and technology."

Broad collection of IP rights: patents, designs, copyrights, trademarks, trade secrets and other
forms, in the U.S. and various foreign countries. Company relies primarily on "the innovative skills,

**Source**: `filings/current/10-K.txt`, Part I, Item 3 (p. 17-18 of the 10-K)
**Fiscal Period**: FY2025 (fiscal year ended September 27, 2025)
**Extraction Date**: Shift 11
**Extracted by**: extractor_1

## Summary

Apple discloses four categories of legal proceedings: (1) EU Digital Markets Act investigations, (2) a
US Department of Justice civil antitrust lawsuit, (3) the Epic Games litigation, and (4) other
ordinary-course proceedings. The two most financially material are the DMA matters (a €500M fine
already imposed plus a second investigation carrying a fine ceiling of **up to 10% of annual worldwide
net sales**, i.e. up to roughly $41.6B on FY2025 revenue) and the Epic Games injunction, which
directly attacks App Store commission economics.

The 10-Q (`AAPL_10-Q_20260627_legal_proceedings.md`) carries these forward with two material
escalations: the Ninth Circuit has instructed the district court to amend the injunction to allow
Apple to charge a commission, and Apple remains under a US court order preventing it from imposing
any commission or fee on certain purchases.

## Key Disclosures

### 1. EU Digital Markets Act — Article 5(4) Investigation
- **March 25, 2024**: European Commission opened a formal noncompliance investigation under
  Article 5(4) of the EU DMA
- Subject matter: how developers may communicate and promote offers to end users for apps
  distributed through the App Store, and how developers may conclude contracts with those end users
- **April 23, 2025**: Commission **fined the Company €500 million** and issued a **cease and desist
  order** requiring Apple to remove technical and commercial restrictions preventing developers from
  steering users to alternative distribution channels outside the App Store
- **Apple has appealed** the Article 5(4) decision

### 2. EU DMA — Article 6(4) Investigation
- **June 24, 2024**: Commission opened an additional formal investigation into whether Apple's new
  contractual requirements for third-party app developers and app marketplaces violate the DMA
- **April 23, 2025**: Commission issued **preliminary findings**
- **Financial exposure**: if the Commission makes a final determination of violation it can issue a
  cease and desist order and "may impose fines up to 10% of the Company's annual worldwide net sales"
  (i.e. up to ~$41.6B based on FY2025 net sales of $416,161M)
- The Commission may seek **additional fines** if it deems Apple violated a cease and desist order
- Apple's position: "The Company believes that it complies with the DMA and has continued to make
  changes to its compliance plan in response to feedback and engagement with the Commission."

### 3. Department of Justice Lawsuit
- **March 21, 2024**: DOJ plus a number of state and district attorneys general filed a **civil
  antitrust lawsuit in the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey**
- Allegations: monopolization or attempted monopolization in the markets for **"performance
  smartphones"** and **"smartphones"** in violation of US antitrust laws
- **Relief sought: equitable relief** to redress alleged anticompetitive behaviour (note: no monetary
  damages sought by DOJ in the disclosed description)
- **Additionally**, various civil litigation matters have been filed in state and federal courts in
  the US alleging similar violations and **seeking monetary damages and other nonmonetary relief**
- Apple's position: "The Company believes it has substantial defenses and intends to vigorously defend
  itself."

### 4. Epic Games
- **Filed**: US District Court for the Northern District of California ("California District Court"),
  by Epic Games, Inc., alleging violations of federal and state antitrust laws and California's unfair
  competition law based on Apple's operation of its App Store
- **2021 Injunction**: the California District Court found certain provisions of Apple's App Review
  Guidelines violate California's unfair competition law and enjoined Apple from prohibiting developers
  from including in their apps buttons, external links or other calls to action directing customers to
  purchasing mechanisms other than Apple's in-app purchase system. Applies to apps on the **US
  storefronts of the iOS and iPadOS App Stores**
- **January 16, 2024**: Apple implemented a plan to comply and filed a statement of compliance
- **September 30, 2024**: Apple filed a motion to narrow or vacate the 2021 Injunction
- **April 30, 2025**: California District Court found Apple **in violation of the 2021 Injunction**
  and enjoined Apple from: (a) imposing any commission or any fee on purchases consumers make outside
  an app; (b) restricting, conditioning, limiting or prohibiting how developers guide consumers to
  purchases outside an app; (c) otherwise interfering with a consumer's choice to proceed in or out of
  an app
- The court **denied** Apple's motion to narrow or vacate, and **referred Apple to the U.S. Attorney
  for the Northern District of California to determine whether criminal contempt proceedings are
  appropriate** — an unusual and material escalation
- Apple appealed to the **Ninth Circuit Court**; the request to stay the decision pending appeal was
  **denied**; the Ninth Circuit agreed to hear the appeal on an **expedited basis, with oral arguments
  heard in October 2025**
- Apple's position: "The Company will continue to vigorously defend its actions and employees"

### 5. Other Legal Proceedings
- Various proceedings and claims arising in the ordinary course, not fully resolved
- **The Company settled certain matters during Q4 FY2025 that did not individually or in the
  aggregate have a material impact on the Company's financial condition or operating results**
- Standard contingency language: outcome of litigation is inherently uncertain; resolution against
  the Company for amounts above management's expectations could materially adversely affect results for
  that reporting period

## Quantitative Data

| Matter | Amount | Certainty | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| DMA Art. 5(4) fine (imposed 2025-04-23) | €500 million | **Determined** | Item 3 |
| DMA Art. 6(4) maximum fine | up to 10% of annual worldwide net sales (~$41.6B on FY2025 net sales) | Contingent on final determination | Item 3 |
| DMA Art. 6(4) additional fines for CDO breach | Not quantified | Contingent | Item 3 |
| DOJ civil antitrust suit | Equitable relief sought (no quantified damages disclosed) | Contingent | Item 3 |
| Other US state/federal antitrust suits | Monetary damages + nonmonetary relief, unquantified | Contingent | Item 3 |
| Epic Games injunction | Commission/fee prohibition on off-app purchases — revenue impact unquantified | In effect, under appeal | Item 3 |
| Q4 FY2025 settlements | Not material individually or in aggregate (no amount disclosed) | Resolved | Item 3 |

## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **The €500M DMA fine is the only quantified adverse legal determination.** No loss contingency
   accrual for it is disclosed in the litigation note text. **Checker should confirm from the
   Commitments and Contingencies note whether the €500M was expensed/accrued and in which period.**
2. **The DMA Art. 6(4) ceiling of 10% of worldwide net sales** is the single largest quantified
   contingent exposure in the filings. It is contingent on a final determination that has not
   occurred. Note that preliminary findings are not a final determination.
3. **Criminal contempt referral** in the Epic Games matter is an unusual disclosure and is not
   quantified. The 10-Q shows the injunction remains operative, which directly threatens App Store
   commission revenue.
4. **The DOJ seeks equitable relief only** as described — but the parallel private suits seek
   monetary damages. The distinction matters for exposure modelling and should be preserved.
5. Apple discloses **no accrued loss contingency amounts** in Item 3 itself. The 10-Q Note 9
   states management's opinion that "there was not at least a reasonable possibility the Company may
   have incurred a material loss, or a material loss greater than a recorded accrual, concerning loss
   contingencies for asserted legal and other claims." This appears to be **in tension** with the
   €500M fine actually imposed and the 10%-of-sales ceiling. Flag for checker.
6. Apple states it **settled certain matters in Q4 FY2025** but gives no amount — only that they were
   not material. The identity of those matters is not disclosed.
"})

## Summary

Item 1B is nil. The cybersecurity disclosure describes a mature, board-overseen security function
with a named executive owner, a dedicated supplier-trust team, and escalation to the Audit
Committee — and, notably for diligence, **no material cybersecurity incidents are disclosed**.
Item 2 Properties is thin: Apple does not itemise its owned versus leased real estate or give
square footage, unlike most registrants. It states only that it owned or leased facilities and land
for corporate functions, R&D, data centres, retail and other purposes worldwide.

## Key Disclosures

### Item 1B — Unresolved Staff Comments
**None.** (Verbatim: "Item 1B. Unresolved Staff Comments None.")

### Item 1C — Cybersecurity

**Governance and accountability**
- Management, led by the **Head of Corporate Information Security**, has overall responsibility for
  identifying, assessing and managing material risks from cybersecurity threats
- The Head of Corporate Information Security has **over 25 years of experience** in the cybersecurity
  industry, including leadership positions at other large technology companies, and has led Apple's
  Information Security team **since 2016**
- Head of Corporate Information Security is **not** a named executive officer or signing officer of
  the filing — the filing is signed by Kevan Parekh, SVP and CFO

**The Information Security team**
Develops and distributes information security policies, standards and procedures; engages in employee
cybersecurity training; implements security controls; assesses security risk and compliance posture;
monitors and responds to security events; executes security testing and assessments. Coordinates with
teams across the company to prevent, respond to and manage security incidents, and engages third
parties as appropriate to assess, test or otherwise assist with security processes and incident
response.

**Third-party / supply chain**
- A dedicated **Supplier Trust** team manages information security risks arising through **supplier
  relationships**
- Processes exist to log, track, address and escalate — for further assessment and report as
  appropriate — cybersecurity incidents **across the Company and its suppliers** to senior management
  and the **Audit Committee** of the Board

**Enterprise risk management**
- The enterprise risk management programme is designed to identify, assess and monitor the Company's
  business risks, including **financial, operational, compliance and reputational risks**, and
  reflects management's assessment of cybersecurity risks

**Board oversight**
- The **Audit Committee assists the Board in oversight and monitoring of cybersecurity matters**
- The Audit Committee **regularly reviews and discusses** cybersecurity risks with management,
  including the Head of Corporate Information Security, the General Counsel, and the Heads of
  Compliance and Business Conduct, Business Assurance, and Internal Audit
- The Audit Committee receives updates as necessary regarding cybersecurity incidents
- The **Chair of the Audit Committee regularly reports the substance of such reviews and discussions
  to the Board**, as necessary

**Incidents**
- **No material cybersecurity incidents are disclosed.** The filing describes processes and governance
  but discloses no material incident, and there is no statement that one occurred or was
  determined not to be material — the disclosure simply contains no incident disclosure.

### Item 2 — Properties
- **Headquarters located in Cupertino, California**
- As of **September 27, 2025**, the Company **owned or leased facilities and land** for corporate
  functions, **R&D, data centers, retail and other purposes** at locations **throughout the U.S. and
  in various places outside the U.S.**
- Company believes its existing facilities and equipment, **which are used by all reportable
  segments**, are in **good operating condition** and **suitable for the conduct of its business**

## Quantitative Data

| Metric | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Unresolved SEC staff comments | None | Item 1B |
| Cybersecurity executive tenure leading InfoSec team | since 2016 | Item 1C |
| Cybersecurity executive industry experience | over 25 years | Item 1C |
| Material cybersecurity incidents disclosed | 0 | Item 1C (absence of disclosure) |
| Dedicated supplier security team | Yes ("Supplier Trust") | Item 1C |
| Board-level cybersecurity oversight | Audit Committee; Chair reports to Board | Item 1C |
| Owned/leased property detail (sq ft, owned vs leased split, per-segment) | **Not disclosed** | Item 2 |

## Red Flags / Items for Checker

1. **Item 2 Properties is unusually sparse.** Apple gives no square footage, no owned-versus-leased
   breakdown, no site list and no per-segment allocation — only the assertion that facilities are in
   good condition. This is a disclosure gap, not a red flag per se, but the checker should not expect
   property-level diligence from this filing; it must come from other sources.
2. **No material cybersecurity incident disclosure.** The absence is consistent with SEC reporting
   thresholds, but the diligence implication is that any material incident would have to be sourced
   from press reports or the 8-K stream, not from the 10-K.
3. **Item 1C contains no statement about ransomware, data breach materiality, or third-party
   (e.g. supply chain) incidents** — supply chain risk is covered operationally by Supplier Trust but
   with no incident history.
4. **The Head of Corporate Information Security is not an officer** and the cybersecurity disclosure
   is not signed off by him personally. This is permitted but worth noting when assessing governance
   depth relative to peers.
5. Item 2 does **not** state that the company owns its headquarters or campus, only that headquarters
   is "located in" Cupertino. Do not characterise the Apple Park campus as owned without another
   source.

## 2. CHANGE OF CONTROL - THE CORE TERM

### 2.1 The trigger (Section 1, definition of "CHANGE OF CONTROL")
A Change of Control is the occurrence of **any one or more** of four events:

**(i) Acquisitions of 50% - a majority-of-shares/board test**
An acquisition by an "Acquirer" of beneficial ownership of **50% or more** of either
(1) the outstanding common stock, or (2) the combined voting power of the outstanding voting
securities. **Four carve-outs** mean this is NOT a Change of Control:
1. any acquisition **directly from the Company**;
2. any acquisition **by the Company**;
3. any acquisition **by any employee benefit plan** (or related trust) sponsored or maintained by
   the Company or an entity it controls; or
4. any acquisition by an entity pursuant to a transaction that complies with the "substantially the
   same proportions" test in limb (iii) (the whitewash/merger-agreement carve-out).

**(ii) Board composition - a board-control test**
A change in the composition of the Board such that the individuals who, **as of February 13, 2018**,
constitute the Board (the **"Incumbent Board"**) **cease for any reason to constitute at least a
majority of the Board**. Two provisos:
- Anyone joining the Board after 2018-02-13 whose election or nomination was approved by a vote of
  at least a majority of those Board members who were also Incumbent Board members is **deemed** an
  Incumbent Board member; **but**
- anyone whose initial assumption of office results from an **actual or threatened election
  contest or proxy/contention solicitation by or on behalf of an Acquirer other than the Board is
  expressly NOT** an Incumbent Board member.

This is a **hard majority test with a frozen 2018 reference date** - a legacy feature of a plan
adopted when the Board was the 2018 slate. It is a notably "entrenched" formulation compared with
a current-market plan, and it is worth flagging to the client.

**(iii) Business combinations - a whitewash test (the most important limb)**
The consummation of a reorganisation, merger, statutory share exchange or consolidation, similar
transaction, or sale/disposition of all or substantially all assets, or the acquisition of assets or
securities by the Company or a Subsidiary (a **"Business Combination"**) - **unless** all three of
the following are satisfied:
1. the pre-Combination owners of common stock and voting securities must **own, directly or
   indirectly, more than 50%** of the shares and more than 50% of the combined voting power of the
   resulting entity, **in substantially the same proportions as their pre-Combination ownership**;
2. **no Acquirer** (other than the resulting entity or an employee benefit plan) may own 50% or more
   of the resulting entity, **except to the extent such ownership existed pre-Combination**; and
3. **at least a majority of the board of the resulting entity** must have been Incumbent Board
   members **at the time of execution of the initial agreement** (or the Board action) providing
   for the Business Combination.

**Limb (iii) is the operative M&A provision.** It is a **whitewash / no-CoC-in-arms-length-deal
carve-out**: if the three-part test is met, the transaction does **not** trigger a Change of
Control. In practice this means a **merger with a stock component where existing Apple holders
retain >50% on a proportionate basis, no acquirer crosses 50%, and a majority of the surviving
board was drawn from the 2018 Incumbent Board will NOT be a Change of Control.**

**(iv) Complete liquidation or dissolution approved by shareholders.**

This is the key economic term:

> **Upon the occurrence of any Change of Control, any then outstanding Award automatically shall
> become vested or exercisable, as the case may be, with respect to a pro rated portion of the
> number of Shares subject to such Award.**

Acceleration is **pro rata, NOT full**. There is a separate "cliff-vesting awards" treatment (and
implicitly a treatment for other awards) referenced at Section 8(a), which continues below.

**Diligence conclusion on vesting**: executive equity accelerates **proportionately on a Change of
Control, not in full** - and in a qualifying stock merger (limb (iii) whitewash satisfied) it does
**not accelerate at all**. This is a more employee-friendly-to-the-company structure than a
typical full-vesting-on-CoC plan. It substantially narrows the speculative equity acceleration
exposure I raised in Shift 9 as a possible concern.

## 3. SHARE LIMIT AND OVERALLOTMENT MECHANICS

**Share Limit: 44,800,000 Shares** (the "Share Limit"), issuable as authorised and unissued shares,
**subject to the provisions of Section 7** (the adjustment provisions, which can move the limit).

**Share Count - the RSU double-count rule**:
- RSUs count against the Share Limit at **two (2) Shares for every one (1) Share** issued.
- Options count at **one (1) Share for every one (1) Share** to which the exercise relates.
- **Cash-settled awards do not consume the Share Limit** (the shares that would have been delivered
  but for cash settlement are not counted).
- **Forfeited/terminated awards recycle**: shares underlying forfeited or terminated awards become
  available again, **but** a forfeited or terminated RSU is credited as **two (2) Shares** when
  determining recycling - mirroring the issuance double-count.

The double-count is a standard anti-dilution mechanic that effectively halves the number of RSUs the
44.8M Share Limit can actually deliver. For a company of Apple's size it is a legacy and
now-irrelevant ceiling (Apple issues multiple billions of shares annually under a separate
shareholder-approved plan), but it is a **contractual cap on this Plan** and worth noting as a
technical constraint.

## 4. ADJUSTMENT PROVISIONS ON CORPORATE TRANSACTIONS (Section 7)

**Section 7(a) - Adjustment triggers.** Upon (or immediately before) any of the following the
**Administrator** shall **equitably and proportionately adjust** (1) the number/type of Shares that
may be the subject of Awards (**including the Share Limit**), (2) the number/amount/type of Shares
subject to outstanding Awards, (3) the exercise price of outstanding Options, and/or (4) the
securities, cash or other property deliverable on exercise/settlement:
- reclassification, recapitalisation, stock split (including stock split in the form of a stock
  dividend), reverse stock split;
- **any merger, combination, consolidation or other reorganisation**;
- any **spin-off, split-up, split-off or extraordinary dividend** distribution;
- any **exchange of Common Stock or other securities**, or any **similar, unusual or extraordinary
  corporate transaction**.

The purpose is expressly to **preserve (but not increase)** the level of incentives intended by the
Plan and the then-outstanding Awards. Any **good-faith determination by the Administrator** as to
whether an adjustment is required, and its extent and nature, is **"conclusive and binding on all
persons."**

**Section 7(b) - Compliance carve-out.** Adjustments are intended, unless the Administrator
determines otherwise, to be made in a manner satisfying applicable legal, **tax (including, without
limitation, Code Section 409A)**, and accounting (so as **not to trigger any charge to earnings**)
requirements. This is the ordinary "avoid a 280G/409A accounting charge" drafting and is a
**diligence-positive** - it signals Apple structures adjustment mechanics to avoid a charge to
earnings and to keep 409A consequences neutralised.

**Section 7(c)** - Adjustments **"need not be the same for all persons or Awards."** Discretionary
and individualised treatment is expressly permitted; there is no single-formula protection.

A "CHANGE OF CONTROL" is the occurrence of any one or more of four events. Note the Plan's threshold

- **Initial RSU Award** for a director first joining off-cycle: the $310,000-based award from the
  preceding Annual Meeting divided by Fair Market Value on the grant date, multiplied by
  **days remaining in the 365-day period following the most recent Annual Meeting / 365** (capped at
  1). **No Initial RSU Award** if the individual (x) was an employee of the Company or a Subsidiary
  immediately prior to joining, or (y) joins on or after **February 1** following the last Annual
  Meeting
- **Settlement** of vested RSUs occurs as soon as administratively practical and **in all events no
  later than 2.5 months after the applicable Vesting Date** - a fixed settlement deadline that is a
  genuine, if modest, obligation

### Dividend Equivalent Rights
- Credited on each ordinary cash dividend date: per-Share dividend **x total RSUs outstanding on the
  record date** (as adjusted under Section 7)
- **Vested Dividend Equivalent Rights are paid in CASH**; they carry the same vesting, settlement and
  other restrictions as the RSUs to which they relate
- **No crediting** of Dividend Equivalent Rights once RSUs cease to be outstanding on the record date

### Shareholder rights and adjustment
- **No shareholder, dividend (other than Dividend Equivalent Rights), or voting rights** on RSUs or
  underlying Shares until the Shares are actually issued
- No adjustment for dividends or distributions for any share whose **record date precedes** the date
  the director becomes holder of record, except Dividend Equivalent Rights and Section 7 adjustments

date C, the vesting amount is:

    Shares vesting = Shares subject to Award x (days from G through C) / (days from G through V)

**This is straight-line time-acceleration to the pro rata point - it is NOT full vesting.** An
award granted and then changed of control control on its cliff date vests 100%; one changed on day
1 vests a negligible fraction.

### 4.2 Section 8(b) - INSTALLMENT-VESTING AWARDS
Applies where the Award has **multiple scheduled Vesting Dates**. The portion that vests is:

already passed**, not from grant. Note the numerator is deliberately worded "following and
excluding the most recent Vesting Date" and the denominator runs to the **next** vesting date - so
where a Change of Control occurs **immediately after** a vesting date, the numerator is close to

Key findings from the new extract:

- **Change of Control** (Sec 12) is triggered by a majority of the **Incumbent Board** (defined as those who constituted the Board as of 2/13/2018) ceasing to constitute a majority of the Board after a Change of Control. A whitewash carve-out allows a hostile takeover to keep the incumbent majority intact.
- **Vesting on Change of Control** (Sec 8) is **pro rata** (not full) — awards vest proportionally to the time elapsed since grant until the Vesting Date, using a day-count fraction. Installment-vesting awards accrue only the next tranche.
- **Amendment/termination** (Sec 10) gives the Board broad prospective power to amend the Plan (including changing the mix of RSUs/Options and sizing methodology) without shareholder approval, except for increasing the maximum Shares issuable (which requires a vote) and repricing options (which requires a shareholder vote).
- **Director consent** (Sec 10(c)) protects individual directors from adverse amendments to their own outstanding awards.
- **Settlement** of vested RSUs occurs within **2.5 months** of the Vesting Date (Section 4(d)).

The **CEO/Executive plans (EX-10.5, 10.7, 10.8, 10.10-10.15)** remain the outstanding high-priority gap for change-of-control economics. The **Clawback** (10-D-1) and **DMA/EIC** litigation are also noted as material risks.

1: # Risk Factors - Apple Inc. (AAPL)
2: 
3: ## Overview
4: The Company's business, reputation, results of operations, financial condition, and stock price can be materially and adversely affected by a number of factors, whether currently known or unknown. These risk factors are detailed in Part I, Item 1A of the 2025 Form 10-K and Part II, Item 1A of the Form 10-Q for the quarter ended March 28, 2026.
5: 
6: ## Macroeconomic and Industry Risks
7: 
8: ### Global Economic Conditions
9: - Operations and performance depend significantly on global and regional economic conditions
10: - Sales outside the U.S. represent a majority of total net sales
11: - Global supply chain is large and complex; majority of supplier facilities located outside the U.S.
12: - Adverse macroeconomic conditions (slow growth, recession, high unemployment, inflation, tighter credit, higher interest rates, currency fluctuations) can materially adversely affect demand for products and services
13: - Consumer confidence and spending can be materially affected by changes in fiscal/monetary policy, financial market volatility, declines in income or asset values
14: - Uncertainty about economic conditions can significantly impact suppliers, contract manufacturers, logistics providers, distributors, carriers, and developers
15: - Potential outcomes include: financial instability, inability to obtain credit, insolvency
16: - Can lead to increased credit/collectibility risk on trade receivables, failure of derivative counterparties, limitations on debt issuance, reduced liquidity, declines in fair values of financial instruments
17: 
18: ### Supply Chain and Component Risks
19: 
20: #### Supply Constraints and Increasing Costs
21: - Experiencing supply constraints and increasing costs for components
22: - Driven by industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND), and memory (DRAM)
23: - Trends expected to intensify, potentially materially negatively impacting revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations, and financial condition
24: - Actions like price increases may not effectively mitigate negative impacts and may reduce demand
25: 
26: #### Single/Limited Source Suppliers
27: - Certain components currently obtained from single or limited sources
28: - Custom components not commonly used by competitors
29: - New products often utilize custom components available from only one source
30: - Initial capacity constraints may exist for new technology components until supplier yields mature or capacities increase
31: - May not be able to extend or renew supply agreements on similar terms, or at all
32: - May not successfully obtain sufficient quantities from suppliers in a timely manner
33: - Component suppliers may fail, consolidate, or decide to concentrate on common components instead of customized components
34: - Substantially all hardware products manufactured by outsourcing partners primarily in China mainland, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Vietnam
35: 
36: #### Computing Resources and AI/ML
37: - Business depends on access to sufficient computing resources
38: - Demand for cloud computing and AI infrastructure has increased substantially across the technology industry
39: - Constrained supply, extended lead times, and increasing costs
40: - Relies on third-party cloud service providers to meet compute needs
41: - May be unable to secure sufficient capacity on commercially reasonable terms, or at all
42: - If unable to obtain adequate compute capacity timely or at reasonable rates, could limit functionality/availability of products/services, delay new features, or cause significantly higher costs
43: - May over- or under-estimate requirements, resulting in higher-than-expected costs or inability to satisfy customer demand
44: 
45: ## Competition Risks
46: 
47: ### Intense Competition
48: - Markets are highly competitive with aggressive price competition and downward pressure on gross margins
49: - Characterized by continual improvement in product performance and price sensitivity
50: - Frequent introduction of new products and services, short product life cycles, evolving industry standards, rapid adoption of technological advancements
51: - Competitors seek to compete through aggressive pricing and very low cost structures
52: - Competitors imitate products and infringe on intellectual property
53: - Apple has minority market share in global smartphone, PC, tablet, and wearables markets
54: - Some markets have experienced little to no growth or contracted overall
55: - Competitors have broad product lines, low-priced products, large installed bases, and large customer bases
56: - Certain competitors have resources/experience/cost structures to provide products/services at little or no profit or even at a loss
57: 
58: ### Developer Ecosystem
59: - Future performance depends in part on support from third-party software developers
60: - Customer purchase decisions depend in part on availability of third-party software applications and services
61: - Third-party developers may discontinue development and maintenance of software for Apple's products
62: - Developer support depends on perceived benefits compared to competitors' platforms (Android, Windows, PlayStation, Nintendo, Xbox)
63: - Factors affecting developer support: market position, anticipated revenue, expected growth, development costs
64: 
65: ## Product and Technology Risks
66: 
67: ### Product Development and Innovation
68: - Ability to compete successfully depends on continuing and timely introduction of innovative new products, services, and technologies
69: - New products may not achieve market acceptance
70: - Product life cycles are short
71: - Dependence on new product introductions and services growth
72: 
73: ### Gross Margin Volatility
74: - Future gross margins can be impacted by a variety of factors
75: - Gross margins subject to volatility and downward pressure
76: - Products gross margin affected by: favorable/unfavorable costs, product mix, tariff costs, higher costs (including memory)
77: - Services gross margin affected by: higher Services net sales, mix of services, higher costs
78: 
79: ## Geographic and Market Risks
80: 
81: ### Greater China Market
82: - Greater China revenue declined 4% in FY2025 ($64.4B vs. $66.9B in FY2024)
83: - Continued volatility in Greater China market could materially affect results
84: 
85: ### International Operations and Currency Fluctuations
86: - International operations expose the Company to foreign exchange risk
87: - Currency fluctuations can materially affect results of operations and financial condition
88: - The Company uses derivative instruments to partially offset foreign exchange risk, but may not hedge all exposures
89: - No assurance that hedges will offset more than a portion of financial impact
90: 
91: ## Regulatory and Legal Risks
92: 
93: ### Trade Restrictions and Tariffs
94: - Restrictions on international trade can increase cost or limit availability of products and components
95: - Tariff costs have impacted and may continue to impact gross margins
96: - Potential for additional tariffs, trade restrictions, or other governmental actions
97: 
98: ### Legal Proceedings and Claims
99: - Subject to various legal proceedings and claims in ordinary course of business
100: - Outcomes are inherently uncertain
101: - May be subject to fines, penalties, or settlements that could materially affect financial condition
102: - Management believes there is not at least a reasonable possibility of material loss concerning asserted legal and other claims
103: 
104: ### Regulatory Compliance
105: - Subject to various federal, state, local, and international laws and regulations
106: - Non-compliance could result in fines, penalties, or restrictions on operations
107: - Increasing regulatory focus on technology companies, data privacy, and competition
108: 
109: ## Tax Risks
110: 
111: ### Unrecognized Tax Benefits
112: - Gross unrecognized tax benefits: $23.2 billion (September 27, 2025)
113: - $10.6 billion, if recognized, would impact effective tax rate

115: - No assurance that reserves are reasonable or that final outcomes will not differ
116: - Could decrease by up to $6 billion in the next 12 months
117: - Effective tax rate volatility due to changes in unrecognized tax benefits

124: - Subject to potential changes in tax laws and regulations

126: - Deemed repatriation tax payable: $8.8 billion (within 12 months)

128: ## Cybersecurity Risks

130: ### Cybersecurity Threats

142: - Exposed to fluctuations in U.S. interest rates
143: - Impacts investment portfolio and term debt

158: ## Operational Risks

38: ### Supply concentration - the material contractual risk
39: - Most components essential to the business are generally available from **multiple sources**
40: - However, **certain components are obtained from single or limited sources**
41: - Apple **uses custom components not commonly used by its competitors**, and **new products
42:   introduced by Apple often utilise custom components available from only one source**
43: - Apple competes for various components with other participants in the smartphone, PC, tablet,
44:   wearable and accessory markets, so even multi-sourced components are subject to industry-wide
45:   shortage and significant commodity pricing fluctuations
46: - When a component or product uses new technologies, **initial capacity constraints may exist**
47:   until supplier yields mature or capacity increases
48: - **Express contractual risk statement from the filing**: *"The Company has entered into agreements
49:   for the supply of many components; however, the Company **may not be able to extend or renew
50:   agreements for the supply of components on similar terms, or at all**, and may not be successful
51:   in obtaining sufficient quantities from its suppliers or in a timely manner, or in identifying
52:   and obtaining sufficient quantities from an alternative source."*
53: - Further: *"component suppliers **may fail, be subject to consolidation** within a particular
54:   industry, or **decide to concentrate on the production of common components** instead of
55:   components customized to meet the Company's requirements"*
56: - **Restrictions on international trade** can increase cost or limit availability of Apple's
57:   products and of the components and **rare earths and other raw materials** that go into them

62: - At **9/27/2025**: **46%** and **23%** of the total
63: - Mechanics: components sold by Apple to manufacturing vendors generate non-trade receivables.
64:   Apple does **not** reflect these component sales in products net sales; it recognises the gain as
65:   a **reduction of products cost of sales when the related final products are sold**.
66:   *This is effectively vendor financing embedded in the supply chain, and it is concentrated in two
67:   counterparties.*

Available Information The Company periodically provides certain information for investors on its corporate website, www.apple.com, and its investor relations website, investor.apple.com. Business Seasonality and Product Introductions The Company has historically experienced higher net sales in its first quarter compared to other quarters in its fiscal year due in part to seasonal holiday demand. Additionally, new product and service introductions can significantly impact net sales, cost of sales and operating expenses. The timing of product introductions can also impact the Company’s net sales to its indirect distribution channels as these channels are filled with new inventory following a product launch, and channel inventory of an older product often declines as the launch of a newer product approaches. Net sales can also be affected when consumers and distributors anticipate a product introduction. During the third quarter of 2026, the Company announced iOS 27, macOS ® 27 Golden Gate, iPadOS ® 27, watchOS ® 27, visionOS ® 27 and tvOS ® 27, and introduced Siri AI. Macroeconomic Conditions Macroeconomic conditions, including inflation, interest rates, component pricing and currency fluctuations, have directly and indirectly impacted, and could in the future materially impact, the Company’s results of operations and financial condition. The Company is experiencing a period of supply constraints and increasing costs for components driven by factors such as industry supply-demand imbalances for components, including advanced semiconductors, storage (NAND) and memory (DRAM). The Company expects these trends to intensify, which may materially negatively impact the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations and financial condition. Actions, such as price increases, that have been and may in the future be taken by the Company may not effectively mitigate these negative impacts, and may also reduce demand for the Company’s products and materially adversely affect the Company’s revenue, costs, gross margin, results of operations and financial condition.  Tariffs and Other Measures Beginning in the second quarter of 2025, new tariffs were announced on imports to the U.S., including additional tariffs on imports from China, India, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Vietnam and the European Union (“EU”), among others. In response, several countries have imposed, or threatened to impose, reciprocal tariffs on imports from the U.S. and other retaliatory measures. On January 14, 2026, initial results were published of the previously announced U.S. Department of Commerce investigation under Section 232 of the Trade Expansion Act of 1962, as amended, into imports of semiconductors, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and their derivative products, including downstream products that contain semiconductors. The announcement of the initial results of the investigation did not impose any additional tariffs affecting the Company’s products. Separately, on February 20, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court (“Supreme Court”) issued a ruling striking down certain tariffs previously imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act of 1977. The Company has applied for a refund of tariffs paid, following the processes established by U.S. Customs and Border Protection, and has recognized any refunds received as a reduction of products cost of sales. Various modifications to U.S. tariffs have been announced, including the recent imposition of tariffs under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, and further changes could be made in the future, which may include additional measures under the Section 232 semiconductor sector investigation, additional sector-based tariffs, further actions under Section 301, or other measures. Tariffs and other measures that are applied to the Company’s products or their components can have a material adverse impact on the Company’s business, results of operations and financial condition, including impacting the Company’s supply chain, the availability of rare earths and other raw materials and components, pricing and gross margin. The ultimate impact remains uncertain and will depend on several factors, including whether additional or incremental U.S. tariffs or other measures are announced or imposed, to what extent other countries implement tariffs or other retaliatory measures in response, and the overall magnitude and duration of these measures. Trade and other international disputes can have an adverse impact on the overall macroeconomic environment and result in shifts and reductions in consumer spending and negative consumer sentiment for the Company’s products and services, all of which can further adversely affect the Company’s business and results of operations. 10: Apple's risk factors run ~77,000 characters across three risk categories in the order presented:
11: **Macroeconomic and Industry Risks**, **Business Risks**, and **Legal and Regulatory Compliance
12: Risks**. Item 1A is the second-longest part of the 10-K after the financial statements, which is
